newsitem.title: CANADA: Anti-separation side pulls ahead in Quebec - poll.
newsitem.headline: Anti-separation side pulls ahead in Quebec - poll.

text.p: A monthly poll released on Friday showed sentiment against Quebec independence pulling into the lead for the first time since separatists narrowly lost a referendum a year ago.

The Leger & Leger poll, commissioned by The Globe and Mail and the Journal de Montreal, pegged "No" voters at 50.6 percent and "Yes" at 49.4 percent -- precisely the same figures as in the finger-biting Oct. 30 referendum.
"The poll results are good news for federalists," The Globe commented.
"This is the first of the monthly Leger & Leger polls since the referendum to put the No side ahead of the Yes side, even if the result is not definitive because of the poll's margin of error."
In August, the Yes (pro-sovereignty) side had led by 52.5 percent to 47.5 percent, and in June the Yes side led 54.9 to 45.1 percent.
The poll questioned 1,002 people between September 20 and 29, with a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points 95 percent of the time.

And regardless of how they would vote, most Quebeckers do not want another referendum for a while. It found 54.9 percent against a new vote in the next four years and only 38.1 percent for. Seven percent did not respond.

By a decisive margin of 69.7 percent to 21.4 percent, voters also wanted separatist Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard to serve out his mandate -- which if followed would mean no provincial elections at least until 1998.
Under Quebec law a new sovereignty referendum cannot be undertaken before provincial elections are held.
